title: The Next Revolution: AI, Advertising, and the Collapse of Old Media | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 30

metadata.title: The Next Revolution: AI, Advertising, and the Collapse of Old Media | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 30

summary: Craig Moffett and Michael Nathanson assess Apple, cable, wireless, advertising and streaming. The guests correctly anticipate a Google-based Siri partnership and the Paramount-Warner combination, while their cable equilibrium thesis remained unproven through the cutoff. Eisman discloses modest de-risking and repeats invalid GDP-minus-total-capex arithmetic. The closing discussion carefully distinguishes AI labor savings from the fraction suppliers can capture as profits.
assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman with Craig Moffett (telecom, cable and Apple) and Michael Nathanson (advertising and media). Speaker attribution is medium confidence for guest handoffs in unlabelled captions.
framework_points: Demand a catalyst and observable operating improvement for a cheap stock.
Check density, cost per passing and cost per connected customer before extrapolating infrastructure coverage.
Distinguish final customer demand from intercompany value-chain revenue.
Compare willingness to pay with competitive realized price.
Separate a successful transaction forecast from an alleged political motive.
tools_and_charts: Cable subscriber losses, mobile growth and conditional equilibrium
Fiber cost per connected home versus cable acquisition value
T-Mobile valuation and demographic subscriber bridge
Ad-share concentration and linear-TV household reach
Final AI revenue versus capex and labor savings
transcript_cautions: Publication October 20 postdates the Verizon CEO announcement referred to as today; recording date is earlier and not precisely established here.
Attribution uses the guests' coverage specialties and conversational handoffs; brief overlapping assent is not assigned independent forecasts.
The claim of 100% Chinese manufacturing is preserved as a supporting factual error, not the main investment failure.
The two guests admit their expected Google-payment catalyst did not occur.

evidence.title: The expenditures approach to measuring GDP
evidence.finding: GDP measures domestic production and subtracts imports embedded in expenditures; worldwide capex is not a domestic growth contribution.

claims.next_check: Recheck the original data and subsequent realized outcomes.

assumptions: Capex is a spending level, while GDP growth is a period-to-period change.
Real growth, nominal spending, imports and global investment need consistent treatment.
evidence_basis.proof: A $400b investment level contributes no direct incremental growth if the previous year also had $400b. Subtracting that level from GDP growth therefore creates a false residual even before adjusting inflation, imports and foreign spending.

assumptions: The value chain is consolidated and financing injections are distinguished from customer demand.
evidence_basis.proof: Payments between firms inside the chain are one firm's revenue and another's cost. Consolidation cancels them; sustainable aggregate operating surplus requires external revenue above external resource costs.
